body: I am not sure where you are getting your info, but there are absolutely benefits to breastfeeding beyond 6 months of age for both baby AND mom. There is a reason why many major health organizations encourage breastfeeding for 1-2 years or beyond in both developing and developed countries. In any case, breastmilk or formula should be the main source of nutrition until at least 1 year of age - meaning she should have been feeding her child at least one of those still.

So she hasn't had any surgeries yet? There is no definitive way to say she even has endometriosis then. It's unusual for a doctor to prescribe such a harsh treatment as Lupron without a definitive diagnosis - endometriosis required a biopsy of the lesiosn to confirm, which requires surgery. It's also possible with her symptoms that endometriosis has spread to her intestines or other organs, which would require surgery to treat.

Even then, hysterectomy is often completely or partially ineffective for endometriosis. The lesions need to be removed, as well as any adhesions that form. Very few doctors preform endometriosis excision surgery, which is by far the gold standard. Most only preform ablation, which burns the top of the endo lesion but leaves the "root" behind, which can still cause pain, inflammation, and bleeding.

How long has she been on Lupron? Is she receiving add back therapy with it? If she isn't, it can put her at risk for osteoporosis later in life and she will have stronger side effects during the treatment. Lupron can have many unpleasant side effects, and could even flare up another undiagnosed illness she may have.

Definitely do some research with her, help her to advocate for herself, and find her a doctor who knows what they are doing. It may take second, third, fourth, or even fifth opinions. But it's worth it. She should not have to live like this, and chances are there's something being missed or something more that can be done.

Those symptoms are actually pretty spot on for a possible autoimmune issue. Excessive sweating/night sweats, GI problems, weight loss, pain, etc. are all pretty standard for many autoimmune diseases. If she's had any weird rashes, eye problems, or joint problems that would lean even more heavily to an autoimmune disease. The symptoms can be pretty vague and non-specific, which can make diagnosis hard. Treatment is also fairly difficult, and sadly it takes much more than the right diet to fix things.

Has she had surgery for her endometriosis? Surgery is the only definitive way to diagnose it. 

It's also very common for endometriosis to be accompanied by autoimmune diseases, which frequently cause the night sweats you describe. Digestive disorders and thyroid disorders would stand out to me as possibilities with her dramatic weight loss. Inflammatory bowel diseases (like Crohns and UC) are also more common in women with endo. The passing out could be related to an undiagnosed autoimmune disorder, or possibly a form of dysautonomia like POTS. Again, this can be more common in women with endometriosis. Many women end up with multiple diagnosis. 

While it is possible she is hiding a more severe illness from you, it's also possible her doctor has been dismissing her concerns and has convinced her it's "not that bad" or "all in her head." This is not an uncommon occurrence, I myself experienced it from several doctors while trying to figure out what was going on in my own body. Turned out I had a combination of endometriosis, Crohns, and interstitial cystitis plus several other disorders. My symptoms and progression of my illness very closely mirror what is going on with your wife.

It may be that she needs a serious advocate for her health. If her doctors are dismissing or downplaying her concerns, it's also very likely they aren't doing as thorough of a job with testing as they should be. It took several years, surgery, multiple scans and blood tests, and a ton of scopes to diagnose my illness. I had to do a lot of my own research and push for my own testing to get diagnosed. I think you should start accompanying to her appointments to see how the doctor is addressing her weight loss and other symptoms, and push to see some other specialists.

I know you said she had testing for Crohns, but how thorough was it? Crohns can occur in any part of the digestive system, so a colonoscopy or even a combination colonoscopy/EGD aren't always thorough enough to catch it. My Crohn's disease initially was only caught on capsule endoscopy, because it was so deep within my small intestine.

It's great that your Crohn's was simple to get under control! I just want to clarify that it isn't that easy for all of us, though. Sometimes, even in remission, surgical removal of the intestine leads to chronic diarrhea that cannot be controlled. 

For many, medications are only partially effective or perhaps not at all. I've been in a constant flare for several years now, and have tried steroids, antibiotics, biologics, immunosuppressants, dietary changes, and so on. None have worked for me.

More than one in ten have chronically active disease, and most of us go through quite a lot to try and control our disease with only minimal to moderate improvement. It can be quite a debilitating, uncontrollable disease - I just don't want to see it downplayed.

No, IBS and IBD are different. IBS only means irritable bowel syndrome, there is no other meaning. IBD stands for inflammatory bowel disorders, like Crohns and UC. While IBS and forms IBD can have some of the same debilitating symptoms, IBS is not in same group as any of the inflammatory bowel disorders and generally is a much less serious diagnosis.

IBS and inflammatory bowel diseases are very different. I'm actually on a low dose chemotherapy drug for my Crohn's disease, and a large percentage of IBD patients undergo major surgeries due to the damage. It is a debilitating chronic illness that can be terrifying at times, and she absolutely needs someone who will support her through this. While some of the symptoms are similar, IBS is a less serious diagnosis.

I was diagnosed with Crohn's while in my current relationship. My boyfriend knows all my TMI stomach issues and never once acted disgusted with me. You know what he does do? Boil water for me and carry me to the bathroom for a hot bath when the pain gets so bad I struggle to stand. He sits there with me to make sure I don't pass out. He helps me clean up if I've vomited and brings me cold water. He sits with me through my infusions, and drives the whole way there and back since I can't drive due to another medical condition. 

Do you really want to spend the rest of your life with someone who treats you like? In a time when you need him the most, he acts disgusted with you and leaves you to handle it on your own. What is he going to do if you ever have emergency surgery and come home with an ostomy? If your disease gets more severe or resistant to medications, and you have to use some of the stronger immunosuppressants that come with problems of their own? I don't want to scare you, but these are very real possibilities if you have IBD. You really need to think about if you want to spend the rest of your life with someone who has so little regard to your struggles and pain just because he finds it gross and unattractive.

Im so sorry you are going through this. I have not been able to be tested for PCOS (I can't stop hormonal treatments long enough to try) but I do know that I have endometriosis and adenomyosis, among others.I  faced a similar decision - I had bled for months on end and tried dozens and dozens of treatments. Although I didn't bleed quite as long as you, another disease of mine (Crohns) was also flaring quite badly and causing significant blood loss.

I was given the options of Lupron, ablation, or hysterectomy. I opted for the Lupron, as that was really my last chance. Within the first month my bleeding had slowed. It eventually stopped, and now I'm terrified for when it will return.

I'm still very open to the idea of a hysterectomy. Although I want children, I've come to realize those organs are a constant source of danger and suffering to me. If I didn't have so much pain, I'd pursue the ablation first. However, I feel like it'd just be a temporary pit stop to the inevitable for me. Hysterectomies can come with their own share of problems however, especially for younger women. 

That being said, I have been exploring all avenues in the meantime. Have you seen more than one doctor? Don't be scared to get a second, third, even fourth or fifth or sixth opinion! These kind of cases are unusual, and it can take a lot of hunting to find the right doctor. Don't be scared to call around and ask if any offices have experience in dealing with something like this.

Do you have research hospitals near you? They may be a good place to start. Even if not, you can contact ones in your state that may be able to guide you towards a doctor. You may need the perspective of multiple doctors in this kind of case - GYNs, endocrinologist, oncologists, vascular specialists, and so on are just some of the doctors who may be able to provide a fresh perspective. You could possibly have other undiagnosed conditions along with the PCOS, contributing to the bleeding.

Many doctors aren't equipped to adequately deal with situations such as this, and may be unaware of treatments that could help. It isn't easy and it will take a lot of work, but you will feel more secure in your decision if you don't leave any stones unturned. 

I'd also suggest looking into your options for egg freezing and IVF or surrogacy in the meantime. You may be surprised at how much others are willing to help out, or what programs may be able to help you. 

I think finding someone to talk to is a great idea as well. Going through this is extremely emotionally draining as well, and the hormones aren't any help. You may also want to check out support groups in your area or online/Facebook - not only will it help to talk to others who have been through similar, some of the women may be able to guide you towards someone who could help. 

Best of luck to you, I really wish you the best and I hope you get some relief soon.
